tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Cyclists must wear a helmet on this coastal path.
The match might be cancelled beyond any possible doubt.
You need not bring a dish to the potluck if you are short on time.
We can must reserve a table before seven.
She ought to stretch before the morning run.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" marks a hard rule here: helmets are required on the path.

Tip: For non-negotiable rules, use "must" + bare infinitive.

FALSE — "Might" only signals weak possibility, so "beyond any possible doubt" contradicts it.

Tip: Certainty language never sits with "might" or "could".

TRUE — "Need not" correctly removes obligation: the dish is optional.

Tip: "Need not" = no duty; "must not" = prohibition.

FALSE — Stacking "can" and "must" is ungrammatical; English allows only one modal before the main verb.

Tip: Choose ability or obligation — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to" + infinitive correctly advises a sensible warm-up.

Tip: "Ought" always needs "to": "ought to stretch", never "ought stretch".
tasks.solution_overview: This set mixes clear obligation, weak possibility, and a double-modal trap. Read each sentence for one job only: does the modal match the certainty or duty the rest of the sentence claims?

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Visitors must to leave wet umbrellas by the door.
You must not to feed the ducks near the jetty.
The delay may stem from a signal failure on the branch line.
They must have knew about the surprise party earlier.
The results could confirm the hypothesis in every scenario without exception.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Must" takes a bare infinitive: "must leave", not "must to leave".

Tip: Pure modals never take "to" before the main verb.

FALSE — After "must not", use the bare infinitive: "must not feed", not "must not to feed".

Tip: Only "ought" and patterns like "need to" bring "to".

TRUE — "May" hedges carefully: a signal failure is a possible cause, not a proven one.

Tip: Use "may" or "might" when evidence is incomplete.

FALSE — Modal perfect needs a past participle: "must have known", not "must have knew".

Tip: Pattern is modal + have + past participle for past deductions.

FALSE — "Could" expresses possibility, so it cannot guarantee an unconditional outcome "without exception".

Tip: Absolute certainty and a weak modal cannot share one claim.
tasks.solution_overview: Four traps crowd this set: illicit "to" after "must", another after "must not", a wrong past participle in modal perfect, and a weak modal that overclaims certainty. Only the cautious "may" sentence stands.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The post cannot have arrived yet — the box is still empty.
Neighbours might have overlooked the note on the gate.
We ought revise the packing list before we leave.
Guests may request an extra blanket at reception.
The ferry will likely be delayed for certain and without any doubt.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have arrived" is a solid modal-perfect deduction about a past event still unconfirmed by evidence.

Tip: Negative modal perfects deny a past possibility on logical grounds.

TRUE — "Might have overlooked" softens a past deduction — possible, not proven.

Tip: "Might have" + past participle = tentative past speculation.

FALSE — "Ought" requires "to": "ought to revise", not "ought revise".

Tip: Treat "ought to" as a fixed pair before the base verb.

TRUE — "May" here marks permission: guests are allowed to ask for a blanket.

Tip: In house rules, "may" often means "are allowed to".

FALSE — "Will likely" already hedges, so "for certain and without any doubt" clashes with that hedge.

Tip: Strip either the hedge or the certainty claim — they cannot both stand.
tasks.solution_overview: Modal perfects and permission "may" appear alongside one missing "to" after "ought" and one hedge-versus-certainty clash. Check structure first, then whether the strength of the modal fits the claim.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Swimmers must shower before entering the pool.
The forecast must show sunshine, though we have no evidence at all.
She could have posted the parcel before the cut-off.
You need not to renew the library card today.
The coach should reconsider the batting order.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must" correctly imposes a non-negotiable pool rule.

Tip: Safety and hygiene rules almost always take "must", not "might".

FALSE — Strong deduction "must" cannot coexist with "no evidence at all".

Tip: No evidence → use "may"/"might", not "must".

TRUE — "Could have posted" correctly frames a past possibility that remains open.

Tip: "Could have" + past participle = past possibility or missed opportunity.

FALSE — Modal "need not" takes a bare infinitive: "need not renew", not "need not to renew".

Tip: Contrast with main-verb "need to": "You need to renew" vs "You need not renew".

TRUE — "Should" appropriately advises a rethink of the line-up.

Tip: "Should" is the default for measured advice.
tasks.solution_overview: Obligation, deduction, and advice sit side by side. Flag any sentence where a strong modal ("must") is undercut by weak evidence, or where an extra "to" sneaks in after "need not".

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The nurse should have flagged the allergy sooner.
Campers may not light fires after dusk under site rules.
He must sign the consent form before the trial starts.
The clouds might suggest a short shower rather than a storm.
We could shorten the hike if we take the ridge path.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Should have flagged" correctly criticises a past missed duty with modal perfect.

Tip: "Should have" + past participle = past advice not followed / mild reproach.

TRUE — "May not" here denies permission under the rules — a standard reading.

Tip: Context decides: "may not" can mean prohibition or weak negative possibility.

TRUE — "Must sign" correctly imposes a hard pre-trial requirement with a bare infinitive.

Tip: Pure modals take the bare verb — no "to".

TRUE — "Might suggest" hedges an interpretation of the sky without overclaiming.

Tip: Soft epistemic modals protect you when signs admit more than one reading.

TRUE — "Could" correctly marks a feasible shorter route, not a guaranteed outcome.

Tip: Possibility "could" is fine when the sentence does not claim certainty.
tasks.solution_overview: All five are sound: past missed duty, rule-based "may not", hard obligation, hedged interpretation, and feasible optionality. Confirm that each modal’s strength matches the claim and that forms stay clean.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The museum might close early with absolute certainty.
Hosts ought to warn guests about the steep stairs.
They cannot have ignored the fire alarm in the hallway.
You should of updated the packing list after the forecast changed.
Volunteers need not bring their own tools to the park clean-up.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Might" and "absolute certainty" cancel each other out.

Tip: Match modal strength to the adverbial claim — weak modal, weak claim.

TRUE — "Ought to warn" correctly advises a prudent courtesy before guests arrive.

Tip: "Ought to" = strong advice, close to "should".

TRUE — "Cannot have ignored" is a firm negative deduction about a past event.

Tip: Loud evidence + "cannot have" = logical impossibility of the alternative.

FALSE — "Should of" is a spoken mishearing of "should have".

Tip: Always write "have", never "of", after a modal.

TRUE — "Need not bring" correctly lifts the obligation to supply tools.

Tip: Modal "need not" + bare infinitive removes duty without forbidding the action.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch for certainty clashes and the classic "should of" spelling trap. Clean advice, negative deduction, and waived obligation pass; overclaimed "might" and "of" for "have" fail.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Students must have finished the quiz by now — every desk is empty.
You may borrow my spare charger if yours is dead.
She might to join us after rehearsal.
Drivers should check tyre pressure before a long trip.
The cake need not be iced until tomorrow morning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have finished" is a strong past deduction backed by empty desks.

Tip: Evidence in the present often licenses "must have" about the recent past.

TRUE — "May borrow" correctly grants permission.

Tip: Offer/permission "may" + bare infinitive is standard.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "might join", not "might to join".

Tip: Pure modals never take "to" before the main verb.

TRUE — "Should check" is measured advice before travel.

Tip: "Should" softens obligation into recommendation.

TRUE — "Need not be iced" correctly says icing can wait — no present duty.

Tip: "Need not" + bare infinitive (passive or active) removes obligation.
tasks.solution_overview: Permission, advice, deduction, and waived duty are all fine here. The only failure is the stray "to" after "might" — strip it and the sentence works.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They could of left the keys under the flowerpot.
You mustn’t park across the neighbour’s drive.
The trail may become muddy after overnight rain.
We ought have booked tickets earlier.
She needn’t have cooked so much — half the trays went untouched.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Write "could have left", never "could of left".

Tip: "Of" after a modal is always wrong in standard writing.

TRUE — "Mustn’t park" correctly forbids the action.

Tip: "Must not / mustn’t" = prohibition, not "no need".

TRUE — "May become" hedges a weather-linked possibility.

Tip: Soft prediction after rain often takes "may" or "might".

FALSE — "Ought" needs "to": "ought to have booked".

Tip: Even in modal perfect, keep "ought to" intact: ought to + have + PP.

TRUE — "Needn’t have cooked" correctly means she cooked unnecessarily in the past.

Tip: "Needn’t have" + PP = past action done though it was not required.
tasks.solution_overview: Prohibition, weather hedge, and "needn’t have" for unnecessary past effort are clean. Failures are form-only: "of" for "have" and a missing "to" after "ought".

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The lights are on, so someone must be home.
He might have been waiting at the wrong platform.
You should must confirm the reservation by Friday.
Artists may exhibit in the foyer during festival week.
We need not to worry about tickets — the show is free.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present deduction "must be" fits strong evidence (lights on).

Tip: Present continuous evidence → "must" + bare infinitive for now-time certainty.

TRUE — "Might have been waiting" softens a past progressive speculation.

Tip: Modal + have been + -ing = tentative past continuous deduction.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should confirm" or "must confirm" — never both.

TRUE — "May exhibit" correctly allows participation during the festival.

Tip: Permission "may" works for temporary openings and invitations.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "need not worry", not "need not to worry".

Tip: Modal "need not" + bare verb; main-verb "need" takes "to".
tasks.solution_overview: Present and progressive past deductions are fine, as is festival permission. Reject stacked obligation and the illicit "to" after "need not".

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup must taste better once it has simmered a little longer.
She could have been practising piano when you called.
Players ought to arrive forty minutes before kick-off.
You may not take photographs inside the chapel.
They must have forgot the picnic basket in the boot.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must taste" here is a confident prediction based on cooking know-how, not a rule.

Tip: Epistemic "must" can project a near-certain outcome from experience.

TRUE — "Could have been practising" correctly frames an open past continuous possibility.

Tip: Progressive modal perfect softens what someone was doing at a past moment.

TRUE — "Ought to arrive" advises a sensible buffer before the match.

Tip: Keep "to" after "ought" even with time phrases.

TRUE — "May not take" denies permission inside the chapel.

Tip: In posted rules, "may not" often equals "are not allowed to".

FALSE — Past participle required: "must have forgotten", not "must have forgot".

Tip: Irregular verbs still need the participle after "have" in modal perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Four clean lines cover prediction, progressive past possibility, advice, and prohibition. Only the wrong past participle after "must have" fails.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bus might well be late in this fog.
You should have told me about the detour sooner.
He must to have left his scarf on the train.
We needn’t stay for the encore if you are tired.
The painting could be a later copy, though experts disagree.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Might well be" idiomatically strengthens a serious present possibility.

Tip: "Might well" ≈ "it is quite possible / rather likely".

TRUE — "Should have told" criticises a past missed courtesy.

Tip: "Should have" + PP = reproach about what did not happen.

FALSE — No "to" after "must": "must have left", not "must to have left".

Tip: Modal perfect is modal + have + PP — never insert "to".

TRUE — "Needn’t stay" correctly lifts the obligation to remain.

Tip: Contracted "needn’t" + bare infinitive is standard.

TRUE — "Could be" hedges an attribution without claiming proof.

Tip: Soft epistemic "could" fits scholarly disagreement.
tasks.solution_overview: Idiomatic "might well", past reproach, waived duty, and scholarly hedge are all valid. Reject only the illegal "to" inside a "must have" chain.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hikers must not leave litter on the ridge.
She may have been about to call when the signal dropped.
You ought to of packed a spare battery.
They couldn’t have finished the jigsaw already — half the pieces are still on the table.
We should water the seedlings every other morning.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must not leave" clearly prohibits littering.

Tip: "Must not" = do not do this; different from "need not".

TRUE — "May have been about to call" hedges an interrupted near-future-in-the-past plan.

Tip: "Be about to" can sit inside modal perfect for near-miss timing.

FALSE — Write "ought to have packed", never "ought to of packed".

Tip: "Have", not "of", even after "ought to".

TRUE — "Couldn’t have finished" denies a past completion on clear present evidence.

Tip: Visible leftover pieces license a firm negative past deduction.

TRUE — "Should water" advises a regular care routine.

Tip: Habitual advice often takes "should" + bare infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview: Prohibition, nested "about to", negative past deduction, and garden advice pass. The only failure is "of" standing in for "have" after "ought to".

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The choir must have been rehearsing for hours — their voices sound tired.
You may as well take the later train if the earlier one is packed.
She needn’t have to bring dessert; the host already baked two cakes.
They mightn’t have noticed the small print on the ticket.
We should have been leaving earlier to catch the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Progressive modal perfect "must have been rehearsing" fits present evidence of tired voices.

Tip: Tiredness now → strong deduction about continuous past effort.

TRUE — "May as well take" idiomatically recommends the practical option.

Tip: "May as well" + bare infinitive = "there is little reason not to".

FALSE — "Needn’t have to bring" double-marks absence of obligation; write "needn’t bring" or "doesn’t have to bring".

Tip: Pick one no-obligation marker — do not stack "need not" with "have to".

TRUE — "Mightn’t have noticed" softens a past negative deduction.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" is acceptable in informal prose.

TRUE — "Should have been leaving" criticises a past progressive plan that started too late.

Tip: Progressive "should have been + -ing" = we ought to have been in the middle of leaving.
tasks.solution_overview: Progressive modal perfects and idioms like "may as well" are legitimate. Reject only the redundant "needn’t have to" pairing — one waived-duty marker is enough.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The battery must be dead — nothing lights up when I press the switch.
He could have been going to apologise before the argument flared again.
You mustn’t have borrowed my bike without asking — and the lock is still on it.
She ought to have been practising scales daily, not only before exams.
We may to have misread the trail markers in the dusk.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present "must be" is a strong deduction from immediate evidence.

Tip: Dead indicators + "must" = confident now-time conclusion.

TRUE — "Could have been going to apologise" hedges an aborted past intention.

Tip: "Be going to" can nest under modal perfects for plans that never landed.

TRUE — Here "mustn’t have borrowed" works with evidence that the lock is untouched, denying the past act.

Tip: Context matters: past "must not have" can deny an action that did not occur.

TRUE — "Ought to have been practising" criticises a past continuous habit that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

FALSE — "May to have" inserts an illegal "to" after the modal.

Tip: Pattern is "may have misread", never "may to have".
tasks.solution_overview: Nested "be going to", progressive "ought to have been", and evidenced "mustn’t have" are advanced but valid. Fail only the stray "to" after "may".

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The garden cannot but have suffered after three weeks without rain.
You should of been checking the oven timer more carefully.
They may well have taken the scenic route to avoid the motorway.
We needn’t have reserved seats — the hall was half empty.
She must can speak Spanish after a year in Madrid.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot but have suffered" is a formal idiom meaning "must inevitably have suffered".

Tip: "Cannot but" + bare infinitive / perfect signals inevitability.

FALSE — "Should of been" must be "should have been".

Tip: Same rule every time: "have", never "of".

TRUE — "May well have taken" strengthens a serious past possibility.

Tip: "May well have" = "it is quite possible that … did".

TRUE — "Needn’t have reserved" correctly means the past reservation was unnecessary.

Tip: Empty hall now proves the earlier booking was surplus.

FALSE — "Must can" stacks two modals; write "must be able to speak" or "can speak".

Tip: English forbids double pure modals — insert "be able to" if you need ability after "must".
tasks.solution_overview: Formal "cannot but" and "may well have" are acceptable advanced shapes. Reject "of" for "have" and the illegal double modal "must can".

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup should have been simmering gently, not boiling hard.
He might have left already, but we cannot be sure.
You need not have brought an umbrella — it never rained.
They mustn’t of crossed the frozen lake on foot.
We ought to update the shared shopping list before Friday.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Should have been simmering" criticises the wrong past continuous cooking method.

Tip: Progressive modal perfect can target how something was being done.

TRUE — "Might have left" correctly softens an uncertain past deduction.

Tip: Pairing "might have" with "cannot be sure" is coherent hedging.

TRUE — "Need not have brought" correctly marks an unnecessary past action.

Tip: Dry weather after the fact proves the umbrella was surplus.

FALSE — Write "mustn’t have crossed", never "mustn’t of crossed".

Tip: Contractions do not license "of" for "have".

TRUE — "Ought to update" correctly advises a timely list refresh.

Tip: Present advice still needs "ought to" + bare infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview: Progressive past advice, soft deduction, and unnecessary past effort are clean. The single failure is another "of" standing in for "have" after "mustn’t".

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The archivist cannot have been other than delighted by the recovered letters.
You should must label the allergy on the lunchbox clearly.
We ought to have been watering the balcony plants daily in this heat.
He mightn’t have realised the path forked behind the barn.
She need not have to renew the membership until autumn.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have been other than delighted" is a formal double negation meaning she must have been delighted.

Tip: "Cannot have been other than …" = strong positive deduction in formal dress.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should label" or "must label" — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to have been watering" correctly criticises a past continuous habit that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Mightn’t have realised" softens a past negative deduction about awareness.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" fits informal narrative.

FALSE — "Need not have to renew" double-marks waived duty; write "need not renew" or "does not have to renew".

Tip: One no-obligation marker is enough.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal double-negative deduction and progressive "ought to have been" are legitimate. Reject stacked obligation ("should must") and the redundant "need not have to" pairing.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The ranger cannot but have noticed the abandoned campfire.
We should have had the boots resoled before the trek.
She may to have understated how steep the final climb was.
Flatmates mustn’t have taken cash from the jar overnight — and the note count proves they did not.
The guide might well have taken a shortcut through the orchard.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot but have noticed" means "must inevitably have noticed".

Tip: "Cannot but" + perfect is formal but grammatical for inevitability.

TRUE — "Should have had … resoled" correctly frames a past causative expectation.

Tip: Modal perfect can wrap causative "have + object + past participle".

FALSE — "May to have" inserts an illegal "to" after the modal.

Tip: Pattern is "may have understated", never "may to have".

TRUE — Here "mustn’t have taken" works as a past prohibition reading supported by evidence that the cash is untouched.

Tip: Context and corroboration matter with past "must not have".

TRUE — "Might well have taken" idiomatically strengthens a serious past suspicion.

Tip: "Might well have" = "it is quite possible that … did".
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced idioms ("cannot but", "might well have") and causative modal perfects are acceptable. Reject only the stray "to" after "may". Read past "mustn’t have" carefully against the evidence clause.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef must have been about to plate the dessert when the power cut hit.
You needn’t to have packed both jumpers and a heavy coat.
They could have been going to cycle the coastal path before the wind rose.
The map should not of omitted the footbridge over the creek.
We may as well have walked for all the good the crowded bus did.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Must have been about to plate" correctly deduces an imminent past plan interrupted by the outage.

Tip: "Be about to" can sit inside a modal perfect for near-future-in-the-past deductions.

FALSE — Drop the "to": "needn’t have packed", not "needn’t to have packed".

Tip: Modal "need not/needn’t" never takes "to" before the verb chain.

TRUE — "Could have been going to cycle" hedges a past intention that never completed.

Tip: "Be going to" can nest under modal perfects for aborted plans.

FALSE — "Should not of omitted" must be "should not have omitted".

Tip: Same rule every time: "have", never "of".

TRUE — "May as well have walked" idiomatically means the bus achieved nothing useful.

Tip: "May as well have" + past participle = ironic "it would have made little difference".
tasks.solution_overview: Nested near-future and "be going to" inside modal perfects are advanced but valid. Failures are form-only: an extra "to" after "needn’t" and another "of" for "have". The ironic "may as well have" idiom is fine.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The volunteers cannot have been other than exhausted after the night shift at the shelter.
She should must escalate any safety concern to the site supervisor the same day.
We ought to have been updating the trail conditions continuously, not weekly.
He mightn’t have realised the ferry required advance booking in peak season.
The book club need not have to maintain two separate reading lists after the groups joined.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Cannot have been other than exhausted" means they must have been exhausted.

Tip: Formal "cannot have been other than …" = strong positive deduction.

FALSE — "Should must" stacks two obligation modals.

Tip: Use "should escalate" or "must escalate" — never both.

TRUE — "Ought to have been updating" correctly criticises a past continuous practice that fell short.

Tip: Progressive past advisability: ought to + have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Mightn’t have realised" softens a past negative deduction about awareness.

Tip: Contracted "mightn’t have" is acceptable in less formal prose.

FALSE — "Need not have to maintain" double-marks absence of obligation; write "need not maintain" or "do not have to maintain".

Tip: Pick one no-obligation marker — "need not" or negated "have to", not both stacked.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal double-negative deduction and progressive "ought to have been" are legitimate advanced shapes. Reject stacked obligation ("should must") and the redundant "need not have to" pairing — one marker of waived duty is enough.
